effect_estimate.comment: Quantitative empirical estimates across all three essays. Note: PDF pp. 1–103 of 180 were visible in the source text (covering Abstract, Ch. 1, complete Essay 1 including Tables 2.1–2.4, and Essay 2 text through Section 3.7; Essay 2 tables and Essay 3 main body on PDF pp. 104–180 were truncated, so Essay 3 estimates come from the Abstract and Section 1.1.3).
effect_estimate.value: Essay 1 (N = 576 state-years, 48 contiguous states, 2000–2011): In the preferred Spatial Durbin Model with random effects and year fixed effects, SDWA health-based drinking water quality violations (% of state population served by PWSs violating MCL or TT standards) are positively associated with real per capita health care expenditures (direct elasticity = 0.005, p = 0.008; indirect neighboring-states elasticity = 0.035, p = 0.003; total elasticity = 0.040, p = 0.003), meaning a 1% reduction in population exposed to violations is associated with a 0.005% ($0.32) in-state and 0.035% ($2.26) regional decrease in annual per capita health care expenditures (non-spatial FE/RE models with year FE were statistically insignificant: FE = 0.000, p = 0.910; RE = 0.001, p = 0.705). Essay 2 (N = 1,985 residential sales, Marion County, WV): In Spatial Lag Models, boil water notices (BWNs) in the year before sale depreciate house prices between 0.57% and 18% depending on the measure—specifically, 1 additional BWN episode reduces house value by 7% direct (1.3% indirect), 1 additional day of average BWN duration reduces value by 2.7% direct (0.6% indirect), binary BWN presence reduces value by 18% direct (3.5% indirect), and a 1-day/year BWN reduction yields a mean total MWTP of $1,160 per house (0.86% of mean price) and $4.60 million countywide; 2SLS spatial quantile regressions show significant negative effects only at quantiles 0.1–0.6 ($2,100–$2,700 MWTP/day at low quantiles; $850–$1,000 at mid quantiles) and null effects at quantiles >= 0.7. Essay 3 (N = 110 WV PSDs): PSDs using multiple raw water sources charge ~29% higher residential water rates per 4,500 gallons than single-source PSDs (implying multi-source backup policies such as WV Senate Bill 373 of 2014 may raise residential charges), NRCS flood-control impoundment use shows no statistically significant rate difference vs. conventional sources, joint water-plus-sewer provision lowers residential water charges, and higher long-term debt and network length increase charges.

mechanism_certainty.comment: Observational non-quasi-experimental econometric study appraised with JBI Analytical Cross Sectional Checklist (design ceiling <= 2). The dissertation documents statistical associations between SDWA regulatory violations, public health boil water notices, and utility raw-water/service structures on health spending, house prices, and residential water charges, while inferring rate impacts of WV SB 373 without directly observing administrative implementation processes.

mechanism_flags.comment: Essay 1 examines public water system compliance/violations of federal Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA) health-based regulatory standards enforced via EPA and state primacy agencies (ENFORCEMENT) and interstate regional coordination (political_coordination). Essay 2 examines regulatory Boil Water Notices issued by PWSs and the county health department across 31 fragmented local water systems (ENFORCEMENT, institutional_fragmentation). Essay 3 models residential water charges per 4,500 gallons (BURDEN, fees) across PSDs, testing combined water-plus-sewer vs. single-service utility structure and federal NRCS impoundment reliance (institutional_fragmentation) and discussing WV SB 373 source water protection mandates.

outcome_flags.comment: Essay 1 measures drinking water contamination via SDWA health-based quality violations (service_quality). Essay 2 measures public water supply unreliability via Boil Water Notice episodes, days, and duration caused primarily by water main breaks and leaks (service_reliability, service_quality). Essay 3 directly measures residential water charges per 4,500 gallons across Public Service Districts, and Essay 2 examines defensive expenditures and differential capitalization in low-price homes (affordability).

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: All three essays are quantitative observational regression analyses without a randomized or quasi-experimental intervention comparator: Essay 2 (pooled cross-sectional hedonic spatial lag and quantile regressions of 1,985 house sales, where the author explicitly states on PDF p. 90 'we are not employing a quasi-experimental identification strategy in this study'), Essay 3 (cross-sectional OLS regression of 110 PSDs), and Essay 1 (observational ecological state-year panel Spatial Durbin random-effects regression of ongoing SDWA violation percentages without treatment/control policy shock). Per RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, quantitative observational regressions without a quasi-experimental intervention comparator map to the JBI Analytical Cross Sectional Checklist.

sample_size.comment: Essay 1 uses balanced annual data for 48 contiguous U.S. states over 12 years (2000–2011, N = 576). Essay 2 filters 7,972 Marion County residential sales (5,525 with structures) to 1,985 arm's-length single-family property transactions (2013–2017) linked to 350 usable boil water notices (2012–2016, out of 440 issued). Essay 3 analyzes 110 Public Service Districts across West Virginia.

study_design.comment: Quantitative multi-essay observational econometric dissertation combining state-level spatial panel regression (Essay 1), spatial hedonic and 2SLS spatial quantile property price regressions (Essay 2), and cross-sectional utility rate OLS regression (Essay 3).
study_design.value: Three-essay quantitative observational econometric study: (1) state-level panel regression and Spatial Durbin Model with random effects and year fixed effects; (2) spatial and non-spatial hedonic property price models (OLS with tax district and year fixed effects, Spatial Lag Model, and 2SLS spatial quantile regression); (3) cross-sectional OLS regression
